Access to dental care is a critical component of overall health. Lack of access can contribute to
gum disease, tooth decay and loss, and increased risk of certain diseases. Poor oral health can be

Despite the clear need for access to dental health care, thousands of Mainers enrolled in
MaineCare face significant challenges in finding dental providers who accept their insurance.

national Medicaid average and includes coverage for case management codes. These provisions

10053787:
Testimony in Support of LD 1652 - "An Act To Improve Access to Oral Health Care through Tax Credits for Dental Professionals and MaineCare Reimbursement Reform"
Submitted by Dr. Kailee Jorgenson, DMD Clinical Director, Mainely Teeth
President, Maine Oral Health Centers Alliance May 8, 2025
Senator Baldacci, Representative Meyer, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services:
My name is Dr. Kailee Jorgenson, DMD. I serve as the Clinical Director at Mainely Teeth and as President of the Maine Oral Health Centers Alliance. I am writing today to express my strong support for LD 1652, which proposes a targeted and fiscally responsible approach to improving dental care access for Maine's most vulnerable populations through the MaineCare program.
Maine faces a well-documented shortage of dental professionals willing or able to accept MaineCare patients. Low reimbursement rates and high overhead costs create a disincentive for participation in the program. LD 1652 addresses this issue on two crucial fronts.
First, the proposed Dental Care Access Credit under �5219-CCC provides a refundable tax credit of up to $5,000 to Maine-licensed dental professionals who are active MaineCare providers. This credit offsets real-world costs such as licensing and malpractice insurance--two significant expenses that can discourage dentists from serving low-income patients. By easing this financial burden, the bill encourages more providers to remain enrolled in MaineCare and actively see Medicaid patients.
Second, LD 1652 directs the Department of Health and Human Services to amend reimbursement rules so that MaineCare payments for dental services more closely align with commercial benchmarks. Reimbursing at 75% of the national commercial rate and covering all dental case management codes are essential reforms to ensure that participation in the MaineCare program is both sustainable and competitive. These changes would help dental practices offset the true cost of care, support comprehensive treatment planning, and improve access for patients who often face long wait times or travel great distances for basic dental services. Serving MaineCare patients frequently involves additional barriers--such as missed appointments, greater care coordination needs, and administrative burdens--that disproportionately impact both providers and patients. These proposed changes would significantly reduce those barriers and provide

vital support to dental offices working to ensure their patients can complete necessary treatment in a timely and effective manner.
By coupling direct financial relief with structural reform of reimbursement policies, LD 1652 offers a comprehensive solution to a growing public health challenge. The bill also includes appropriate safeguards and transparency, such as certification requirements and annual reporting by DHHS and the Bureau of Revenue Services.
This legislation is a critical investment in Maine's dental infrastructure and will help ensure that children, seniors, and low-income families can access the routine and preventive oral health care they need.
I urge the committee to vote Ought to Pass on LD 1652. Thank you for your time and your commitment to improving health care access in Maine.
Respectfully submitted, Dr. Kailee Jorgenson, DMD Clinical Director, Mainely Teeth President, Maine Oral Health Centers Alliance
10053446:
Testimony of Kalie Hess, Associate Director Children's Oral Health Network of Maine
LD 1652: An Act to Create a Tax Credit for Providers of Dental Care for MaineCare Recipients Before the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation Public Hearing: May 8, 2025
Good afternoon, Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation. My name is Kalie Hess, and I am here today on behalf of the Children's Oral Health Network of Maine (COHN) to ask for your support on LD 1652.
COHN is a network of trusted organizations and individuals united by a shared vision: a Maine where all children grow up free from preventable dental disease. Despite limited resources, our partners work creatively and persistently to bring quality oral health care to children across the state, even as we face a growing oral health crisis. While much of our legislative work falls under the Health and Human Services Committee, we are grateful for the opportunity to speak with you today about why LD 1652 is a critical part of addressing this crisis. We were part of the MaineCare Task Force discussions that resulted in this bill, and we appreciated the collaborative effort to address the challenges together with all of the other partners who came together in the task force.
Maine is facing an acute shortage of oral health providers, particularly for children and families enrolled in MaineCare. Currently, only about one in five children with MaineCare have an active dental home, meaning a dental office where they have been able to get at least one cleaning and one exam a year.1 Many of us would consider that the bare minimum of oral health care, but even that is out of reach for most MaineCare-enrolled children.
One major barrier to recruiting dental providers to enroll with MaineCare is the significant administrative burden they face when working with MaineCare: outdated billing systems, communication challenges, delays and hoops to jump through for reimbursement, and a lack of a clear point of contact for dental-related issues. These challenges are so substantial that stakeholders worked with the Office of MaineCare Services to create a Dental Subcommittee of the MaineCare Advisory Committee. This subcommittee was meant to help raise concerns, suggest improvements, and provide a space for collaboration, but even with this collaborative structure in place, the responsibility for different elements of the problems and solutions are so fragmented across different roles within MaineCare, none of whom have any specific expertise with how dental care or dental billing works.

1 Fox, K. S., Kumarage, A., McGuire, C., & Stultz, E. (2024). Assessing Maine children's access to a dental home: Dental insurance does not guarantee receipt of dental care. University of Southern Maine, Muskie School of Public Service, Catherine E. Cutler Institute, Population Health & Health Policy. https://www.mainecohn.org/assets/stock/2024-DentalHome-Utilization-Maine-Children.pdf

Children's Oral Health Network | Kalie Hess | kalie@mainecohn.org | www.mainecohn.org

1

This means that there can rarely be a single point of contact identified with dedicated responsibility, and the knowledge and understanding necessary, for implementing solutions. The result is that many urgent issues remain unresolved for months and even years on end. Meanwhile, providers -- many graduating with something like half a million dollars in student loan debt -- must weigh the high costs of practicing in Maine against both the reimbursement rates MaineCare offers and the administrative burden required to recoup that reimbursement. From conversations with our Network partners, with the recent MaineCare reimbursement rate improvements, the administrative burden may now be an even bigger reason why so many are unable or unwilling to accept MaineCare, leaving most children who have MaineCare without access to care for the most common chronic disease of childhood. Without systemic improvements, including more dedicated staff at MaineCare to manage and support the dental benefit, more support for care coordination, and a tax incentive for providers who choose to serve MaineCare patients, we will continue to see the door to oral health care remain locked for far too many Maine kids and adults in every community across Maine. We respectfully ask you to vote Ought to Pass on LD 1652 to help ensure we have a workforce and a public health care system that can more efficiently and effectively serve the children who need it most. Thank you for your time and consideration. I'm happy to answer any questions.

TESTIMONY OF MICHAEL J. ALLEN, ASSOCIATE COMMISSIONER FOR TAX POLICY
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE AND FINANCIAL SERVICES
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation Hearing Date: May 8, 2025
LD 1652 - "An Act to Create a Tax Credit for Providers of Dental Care for MaineCare Recipients"
Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and members of the Taxation Committee - good afternoon, my name is Michael Allen, Associate Commissioner for Tax Policy in the Department of Administrative and Financial Services. I am testifying at the request of the Administration Against LD 1652, "An Act to Create a Tax Credit for Providers of Dental Care for MaineCare Recipients."
This testimony is limited to the bill as it affects taxation and Maine Revenue Services. For tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, the bill proposes a nonrefundable income tax credit for eligible dental professionals. The credit is equal to the dental professional's licensing fees and malpractice insurance costs, up to $5,000. An eligible dental professional must be licensed under Title 32, chapter 143, be an enrolled MaineCare provider, maintain a current and active list of patients for whom reimbursement is received through the MaineCare program, and be certified by the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS). Unused credits may not be carried back or forward to other tax years.
Currently, eligible dentists certified by the Maine DHHS Oral Health Program on or after January 1, 2018, but before January 1, 2023, may be eligible for the dental care access credit under 36 M.R.S �5219-DD. An eligible dentist must agree to practice full-time for at least five years in an underserved area of the State as defined by federal guidelines. The credit may be first claimed in the tax
1

year in which the eligible dentist meets the conditions of eligibility for at least six months and each of the four subsequent tax years, subject to continued eligibility. The maximum credit amounts are: $6,000 for the first year, $9,000 for the second year, $12,000 for the third year, $15,000 for the fourth year, and $18,000 for the fifth year. The credit is nonrefundable and cannot be carried to other tax years. The credit is repealed on December 31, 2027.
The lack of a capped certification process distinguishes this credit from similar credits for attorneys, dentists, and doctors.
Providing this benefit through the tax code creates additional steps and delays for recipients. If current reimbursement rates are too low, alternative approaches, for instance a grant program or legislation targeting the underlying issues may be simpler and more effective and should be considered. In addition, there are many professions with a shortage of workers, and it is not feasible for the State to offer tailored tax credits for every sector of the Maine economy.
The Administration notes the following technical concerns:

The bill should clarify whether an "eligible dental professional" could qualify for both the proposed credit and the current dental care access credit.
� It is recommended that the credit be limited to the licensing fees and malpractice insurance costs paid or incurred during the taxable year.
� The bill requires DHHS to notify MRS whenever a dental professional ceases to meet the conditions of eligibility. It is recommended that

10051806:
Testimony of Dr. Michael Dowling, DMD
In Support of LD 1652 - "An Act to Support Health Care Providers Serving MaineCare Members"
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation
May 8, 2025
Senator Grohoski, Representative Perry, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation:
My name is Dr. Michael Dowling, and I am a board-certified pediatric dentist practicing in Yarmouth, Maine. For nearly 15 years, I've provided care to children and adolescents at 207 Pediatric Dentistry, which serves as a dental home to approximately 10,000 patients. About half of those we serve are covered by MaineCare. I also chair the Maine Dental Association's Council on Government Relations and am a past president of the Maine Society of Pediatric Dentistry.
I write in strong support of LD 1652, "An Act to Support Health Care Providers Serving MaineCare Members." Although this bill is under the jurisdiction of the Taxation Committee, its heart lies in health policy. It is about increasing access to care for low-income Mainers--especially children--and helping ensure there is a strong, stable network of providers willing and able to participate in the MaineCare program.
One important component of this bill is the proposed tax credit for health care professionals who treat MaineCare patients. This is a strategic incentive that acknowledges the realities providers face when participating in a program that has historically paid well below the cost of care. Modest financial offsets through the tax code can make a meaningful difference in retaining existing providers and attracting new ones, particularly in high-need areas. As providers evaluate where to practice and whether to participate in MaineCare, incentives like this matter.
Beyond financial relief, LD 1652 also wisely calls for dedicated staff within MaineCare to assist providers and patients. This is a critical and often overlooked piece of the puzzle. Many practices, especially smaller ones, struggle with the administrative complexity of the program--from eligibility issues and prior authorizations to coding requirements and denials. Having accessible, knowledgeable support staff within MaineCare who can help troubleshoot problems and guide patients through the system would reduce frustration, save time, and ultimately help more people receive the care they need.
Another essential component of this bill is its recognition that reimbursement rates must be increased. While I am proud to continue serving MaineCare families, I can say from firsthand experience that the current rates simply do not reflect the costs of providing care. For many providers, especially those just starting out or managing significant overhead, it is not financially viable to participate fully in the program.

We also know from research that raising Medicaid reimbursement improves access to care. For example: - A 2019 report from the Urban Institute found that increases in Medicaid physician fees were associated with higher rates of provider participation and improved appointment availability for Medicaid patients. - A 2017 study in Health Affairs showed that when Medicaid reimbursement rates for dental services rose to approach commercial insurance rates, children's access to dental care increased significantly. - The U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) has also documented the link between higher Medicaid payment rates and better access to services, especially in primary and specialty care.
LD 1652 takes a holistic approach by combining financial incentives, system-level support, and payment reform. These changes are urgently needed if we are serious about maintaining a robust network of MaineCare providers--and ensuring that Maine's children and families do not face long delays, unnecessary travel, or complete lack of access.
I respectfully urge you to vote Ought to Pass on LD 1652. Thank you for your time, your consideration, and your work to make health care more accessible for all Mainers.
Sincerely, Dr. Michael Dowling 207 Pediatric Dentistry Yarmouth, Maine

Re: LD 1652 - An Act to Create a Tax Credit for Providers of Dental Care for MaineCare Recipients
Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation, thank you for the opportunity to provide information in opposition to LD 1652 - An Act to Create a Tax Credit for Providers of Dental Care for MaineCare Recipients.
This bill (1) establishes a tax credit for licensing and malpractice insurance costs up to $5,000 for dental providers who treat MaineCare patients, (2) requires DHHS to amend its rule Chapter 101: MaineCare Benefits Manual, Section 25, Dental Services and Reimbursement, to reimburse all dental services at 75% of the "national state Medicaid rates" and to provide reimbursement for all dental case management codes, and (3) requires DHHS to create three positions within the office of MaineCare services dedicated to the dental programs and services provided under the MaineCare program.
The Department opposes the bill for several reasons. First, requiring the Department to amend MaineCare's rates circumvents the established rate determination process set forth in 22 MRS 3173-J.
In addition, while the bill overall seems intended to implement changes to increase dental provider participation in MaineCare, setting rates at 75% of the average Medicaid rates nationwide, as the bill appears to require (the bill's language that the Department must reimburse at "75% of the national state Medicaid rates" is not clear and would need clarification if the bill were to be enacted), the bill would actually result in a rate decrease for almost all of MaineCare covered dental codes and a $17.2 million decrease in MaineCare spending ($5.8 million in General Fund) on dental services. Such a decrease in rates would likely discourage dental provider participation in MaineCare and have an adverse impact on MaineCare members' access to dental services. If the description of the rate methodology in LD 1652 represents an error and the intention is to increase reimbursement, the Department is not in the position at this time to do so given the budget shortfall.
Lastly, we do not believe that the bill's requirement that the Department create three positions dedicated to the dental programs - at an estimated annual cost of over $300,000 - is necessary. The Department already has several positions working consistently on dental issues and the Department meets monthly with providers as part of a dental subcommittee to the MaineCare Advisory Committee under the direction of MaineCare Medical Director Courtney Pladsen, and with participation by MaineCare Provider Relations, Policy, and other units, in order to collectively work through identified issues.
The Department would be happy to provide additional information and further discuss the issues associated with LD 1652 and our opposition to moving forward with the bill. Please feel free to contact me if you have any questions during your deliberation of this bill.

Sincerely,
Michelle Probert Director Office of MaineCare Services Maine Department of Health and Human Services

10056637:
Testimony of the Maine Dental Association before the Taxation Committee
In SUPPORT of
LD 1652 An Act to Create a Tax Credit for Providers of Dental Care for MaineCare Recipients
Public Hearing: Tuesday, May 8, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and Distinguished Members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee:
I am Therese Cahill, and I serve as the Executive Director of the Maine Dental Association. The MDA represents all dentists in Maine and is a statewide association dedicated to promoting oral health, advancing excellence in dentistry, and building a future that empowers Maine's communities with sustainable access to oral healthcare. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.
Without question, LD 1652 An Act to Create a Tax Credit for Providers of Dental Care for MaineCare Recipients is perhaps one of the most consequential pieces of legislation for the people of Maine who are eligible for MaineCare and seeking dental care. Due to a myriad of reasons, the shortage of dental providers in our State is significant, and it is even more challenging for those with MaineCare insurance to find a provider to meet their oral health care needs.
We are at a crossroads. While Maine's population has increased approximately 4.3% over the last 5 years, the same does not hold true for new dentists and dental hygienists practicing in our State. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (2023), the number of Maine dentists declined from 590 in 2019 to 530 in 2023, and the number of hygienists fell from 1,040 to 840. The problem gets worse when you consider like the rest of Maine, the dental workforce is aging. In fact, in March 2024, 57% of active licensed dentists were at least 60 years old. This was discussed in an article published in the Portland Press Herald Access to dental care in Maine reaching a crisis point (May 2024). Last year, Maine had six (6) new dental school graduates (5 from UNE, one from Tufts) apply for dental licenses; conversely, we had over 50 dentists retire. This is trend shows no signs of slowing down.
In this same timeframe of the decline mentioned above, the number of dental providers enrolled in MaineCare has also declined, not surprisingly. Add to this, in July 2022, the expansion of the adult dental benefit started, which emphasized this decline. Providers have shared administrative burdens in enrollment and historical issues with submitting and receiving payment for claims, as well as the lower reimbursement rates, are roadblocks to taking any or more patients with MaineCare. The Office of MaineCare and the MaineCare Advisory

Committee's Dental Subcommittee have been discussing how to recruit and retain more dental providers. This legislation takes the concerns expressed dental providers and works to creates solutions to address these issues.
This bill seeks to allow dental providers who care of the oral health needs of people with MaineCare to be eligible for a tax credit of up to $5,000 to offset licensing fees and malpractice insurance. This incentive would be helpful to providers who take a sometimes-significant reduction of their rates when accepting MaineCare an allowance to get credit for necessary costs of providing care.
The second tenet of this bill addresses the overall rate structure. Here, we'd like to correct lines 37-38, which should read "75% of the average commercial rates". Right now, the rates are mostly set at 50% of these commercial rates, with some codes at 67%. By increasing the rates to 75%, and appropriating the State funds to support this, more providers will look at providing care to patients with MaineCare as a more realistic option as they try to run their small businesses.
Lastly, this legislation asks for the addition of staff at the Office of MaineCare to support providers and alleviate the continued and historic issues of enrollment and claim challenges dental providers have run into repeatedly. These small practices often need to hire one person just to manage MaineCare enrollment and billing. Reducing this barrier will go a long way in supporting dental providers who do not have the larger staffs often found at other healthcare provider facilities.
We urge this committee to support the people of Maine and the dental professionals who want to serve them by making an investment in Maine residents' oral health by supporting LD 1652 with the rate amendment. While we are fully cognizant of Maine's fiscal challenges, particularly with MaineCare, we cannot afford to ignore the fact the people who have MaineCare continue to have significant challenges in receiving the oral health care they deserve.
Thank you for your time and attention.

Good afternoon, Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier and distinguished members of the Taxation Committee.
My name is Traci Dempsey, I reside in Bath, I am a dental hygienist of over 25 years and I am the president of the Maine Dental Hygienists' Association representing nearly 1300 dental hygienists in Maine. I am testifying in strong support of LD 1652.
It is no secret that we have an access to dental care problem here in Maine. Maine faces a serious shortage of dental providers willing or able to accept MaineCare due to chronically low reimbursement rates and the disproportionate administrative burdens that come with Medicaid participation. For many providers, the economic disincentives are simply too great to ignore. This bill directly addresses these barriers.
The $5,000 tax credit is a targeted way to recognize and offset the financial burden that often discourages providers from participating in the MaineCare program. Licensing and malpractice insurance are essential, yet significant, overhead costs. By easing this burden, we are encouraging more dental professionals--particularly those early in their careers or working in underserved areas--to participate in the Medicaid system.
Reimbursing at 75% of national commercial insurance rates is a long-overdue correction to an outdated payment structure. Maine has lagged behind many states in ensuring that Medicaid providers are paid fairly, which has led to an access crisis for low-income Mainers. Without adequate reimbursement, providers cannot cover their overhead, invest in new technologies, or dedicate time to complex care needs.
Additionally, expanding reimbursement to include all dental case management codes recognizes the full scope of services dentists and their teams provide. Effective case management improves outcomes, reduces missed appointments, and ensures continuity of care--especially for vulnerable patients with chronic or complex needs.
Finally, this bill wisely calls for the establishment of three new positions within the Office of MaineCare Services dedicated to dental programs. This investment is more than bureaucratic expansion, it is the infrastructure necessary to ensure that these policy improvements are implemented effectively, monitored appropriately, and adapted over time based on data and outcomes.
Oral health is inseparable from overall health. Untreated dental disease leads to increased emergency department visits, worsened chronic conditions, missed school and work days, and, in some cases, lifethreatening infections. By making it easier for dentists to serve MaineCare patients, this bill advances both health equity and fiscal responsibility.

In closing LD 1652. is a comprehensive, pragmatic, and deeply needed step forward. It supports providers so that they can support patients. It adjusts reimbursement to reflect real costs. And it strengthens the state's capacity to manage and grow its dental programs. I urge you to support this bill and help ensure that every Mainer, regardless of income, has access to the dental care they need and deserve. Thank you for your time, and I am happy to answer any questions.
